title: Mode A and Mode B weights
summary: PLS estimates outer weights either from simple correlations (Mode A) or from a multiple regression (Mode B); the mode is an estimation choice that is not the same thing as formative measurement.

body.text: Each PLS construct score is a weighted sum of its indicators. The weights are estimated in one of two ways. In [[mode-a]] each weight is proportional to the correlation of the indicator with the construct's inner proxy, as if each indicator were regressed on that proxy separately. In [[mode-b]] the proxy is regressed on all indicators of the block jointly, so the weights are multiple-regression coefficients.

body.display: Mode A: wᵢ ∝ cor(xᵢ, Z)    Mode B: w ∝ R⁻¹ · r
body.explanation: Z is the inner proxy of the construct. In Mode A each weight is proportional to the correlation of indicator xᵢ with Z. In Mode B the weight vector is the inverse of the indicators' correlation matrix R times the vector r of their correlations with Z, so the weights depend on how the indicators correlate with each other.

body.text: Because Mode B uses the indicators' intercorrelations, collinear indicators make its weights unstable and can even flip their signs; check the indicator [[vif]]. Mode A is unaffected by collinearity within the block.

Mode is an estimation choice, not a theory of measurement. Mode B consistently estimates the weights of a composite model, while Mode A combined with the consistency correction of PLSc matches the reflective common-factor model (Dijkstra 2017). Composites can also be built with Mode A or fixed weights, and a formative construct with causal indicators and its own error term is not a composite at all (Bollen & Bauldry 2011). SEM Studio ties the mode to the declared measurement: reflective blocks use Mode A, composite-formative blocks Mode B; some other programs let you choose.

mistake.title: Treating Mode B as proof of formative measurement
mistake.text: Estimating a block with Mode B does not validate a formative theory, and choosing Mode A for an index is not automatically an error. Justify the measurement model conceptually and report the weighting mode as an estimation decision.

tryIt.task: Run PLS-SEM on this model. On the Results page compare the outer weights of F (Mode B) with those of X (Mode A), and look up the indicator VIFs of F.

checks.question: Which statement about Mode B is correct?

options.text: Its weights are multiple-regression coefficients, so collinearity among the block's indicators affects them.
options.feedback: Correct. That is why indicator VIFs are checked for Mode B blocks.

options.text: It is required whenever indicators are measured on Likert scales.
options.feedback: The response format has nothing to do with the weighting mode.

options.text: It turns any block into a formative construct.
options.feedback: The mode only changes how weights are estimated; whether a construct is formative is a conceptual question.

options.text: It corrects composites for measurement error.
options.feedback: Error correction for common factors is the job of PLSc, not of Mode B.

checks.question: In a Mode B block, indicator f3 has a positive loading but a negative weight. What is the most plausible explanation?

options.text: Collinearity or suppression among the block's indicators; inspect the VIFs and the content before acting.
options.feedback: Correct. Regression weights can change sign when predictors overlap, even if each correlates positively with the composite.

options.text: f3 is reverse-worded and must be reverse scored.
options.feedback: A reverse-worded item would show a negative loading too. Here the loading is positive.
Sign differences between weights and loadings are common in converged solutions; convergence is reported separately.

checks.explanation: Weights and loadings answer different questions in Mode B.
